card.title: Lenz's law and conservation of energy

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Lenz's law chooses the induced current so that it opposes the change in flux. An approaching south pole is met by a south face. The agent must do work against that opposition, and that work is the energy of the induced current. A stationary magnet induces nothing.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
W = F s cosθ
KE = ½mv²
PE = mgh

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Eddy-current brakes use this opposition.  ·  The right-hand grip turns the opposing pole into a current direction.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Lenz's law says the induced current takes the direction that opposes the change in flux which caused it. It is the reason for the minus sign in Faraday's law.  ·  If the south pole of a magnet approaches a coil, the flux of that pole is increasing. The near face of the coil becomes a south pole so that it repels the approaching south pole.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Oppose the change  ·  South-pole approach  ·  Work done by the agent  ·  Eddy-current brake

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Direction, not magnitude.  ·  Oppose the change, not the field.  ·  The agent must do work.  ·  That work becomes electrical energy.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Work W = F·s·cosθ (J); power P = W/t = F·v.  ·  Work-energy theorem: net work = ΔKE = ½m(v₂² − v₁²).

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Where does the electrical energy come from?

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: The south pole of a magnet is pushed toward a coil. Name the pole on the near face and say where the energy of the induced current comes from.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: Lenz's law fixes → B  ·  An approaching south pole induces a near face that is → A

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: If that south pole is pulled away, the flux decreases and the near face becomes a north pole, attracting the magnet and opposing the removal.  ·  The opposition is to the change. A stationary magnet produces no change and no induced current, so there is no force from an induced current.  ·  Pushing the magnet in against the repulsion takes mechanical work. That work is the energy which appears as the induced current's heating in the coil. If the induced current had attracted the magnet, the motion would accelerate and energy would appear from nowhere.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: P = Fv  ·  ❌ skip the key fact → ✅ work w = f·s·cosθ (j); power p = w/t = f·v..  ·  Lenz opposes the change, not the field itself.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: An approaching south pole induces a south face, not a north face.  ·  The law does not give the number of volts.  ·  A stationary magnet induces no opposing force.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Say whether the flux is increasing or decreasing before naming the face.  ·  Connect the force to the energy, not only to the pole.  ·  Write The induced current opposes the change in flux. and say what each symbol means.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Mark the known values, then substitute one step at a time.  ·  Finish with the number, the unit, and the direction when the quantity has one.  ·  Mechanical energy conserved when only conservative forces act: KE + PE = const; PE(mg) = mgh.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: State the limit / condition where a formula or rule stops being valid before applying it.  ·  Limit to remember: work w = f·s·cosθ (j); power p = w/t = f·v.  ·  Eddy currents in a copper plate near a moving magnet oppose the motion and dissipate energy as heat. That is Lenz's law used as a brake.
